# ROCOv2 — radiology images + captions

**Samples:** 24000 figure images from open-access biomedical papers
(PubMed Central), each paired with its **figure caption**, so row *i* is one
image–text pair (paired multimodal data).

| modality | kind | stored as |
|---|---|---|
| `image` | image | JPEG, RGB, shorter side resized to 256 px (aspect kept), path in column `image_path` |
| `text` | text | raw caption in column `caption` (median 17 words, 90th pct 38) |

Most images are grayscale scans stored as RGB. Captions are written by paper
authors for readers, not clinical reports: they often name the imaging
modality, body part and finding, and can mention arrows or panel letters.

## Labels (for evaluation)

- `label`: imaging modality, from ROCOv2's manually curated concepts
  (checked by a radiologist). Images with no or several modality concepts were
  dropped (see below).
- `cuis` / `concept_names`: all automatically extracted UMLS concepts of the
  caption (multi-label; usable as extra evaluation targets).

| label | train | val | test | total |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| CT | 6998 | 791 | 717 | 8506 |
| X-ray | 5581 | 543 | 565 | 6689 |
| MRI | 3299 | 276 | 301 | 3876 |
| Ultrasound | 2746 | 283 | 322 | 3351 |
| Angiography | 1263 | 98 | 82 | 1443 |
| PET | 113 | 9 | 13 | 135 |

## Splits and subset

ROCOv2's own split (train / valid → `val` / test) is kept, so `test` images
come from different papers than `train`. A fixed random subset (seed 0)
of each split is used to keep training laptop-sized:

| split | available with one modality label | kept |
|---|---:|---:|
| train | 59465 | 20000 |
| val | 9773 | 2000 |
| test | 9822 | 2000 |

Fit every preprocessing step and model on `train` only; use `val` for model
choices and `test` for the final numbers.

## Modality concepts used for the label

| CUI | concept | label | images |
|---|---|---|---|
| C0040405 | X-Ray Computed Tomography | CT | 27747 |
| C1306645 | Plain x-ray | X-ray | 21997 |
| C0024485 | Magnetic Resonance Imaging | MRI | 12657 |
| C0041618 | Ultrasonography | Ultrasound | 11429 |
| C0002978 | angiogram | Angiography | 4799 |
| C0032743 | Positron-Emission Tomography | PET | 432 |

## Preparation already applied (not the agent's choice)

- Resizing (shorter side 256 px) and RGB conversion only; no cropping,
  no normalisation, no caption cleaning or tokenisation.

Source: https://zenodo.org/records/10821435 (CC BY-NC 4.0; non-commercial use only; individual images
keep the licences listed in ROCOv2's `license_information.csv`).

name: objective
description: Turn the user's objective into downstream tasks, headline metrics, required baselines, a label-use policy and a falsifiable success criterion.
---

# When to apply
Right after inspecting the data, before any preprocessing or modeling decision.

# Step 1 — map the wording to downstream tasks

| Objective wording | Downstream task | Headline metric (evaluate.py) | What it needs from the representation |
|---|---|---|---|
| "identify / classify / annotate cell types", "classify modality", "predict the label" | classification | `structure` → linear-probe **balanced accuracy** (and macro-F1) on the named label | a joint embedding (or the relevant modality's embedding) |
| "cluster", "discover groups", "unsupervised", "without labels" | clustering | `structure` → k-means **ARI / NMI**, silhouette | a joint embedding trained WITHOUT labels |
| "retrieve", "find the matching caption/image/cell", "search", "match across modalities" | cross-modal retrieval | `retrieval` → **recall@k** both directions, FOSCTTM | one embedding per modality in a SHARED space of equal dimension |
| "predict one modality from the other", "impute", "translate RNA→ATAC" | cross-modal prediction | `cross` → per-sample / per-feature Pearson r (continuous) or AUROC (binary) vs the train-mean baseline | an embedding of the SOURCE modality alone |
| "integrate", "joint representation", "combine modalities" | integration | classification/clustering of the joint embedding **vs each modality alone** | joint + per-modality embeddings |
| "does modality X add information?" | ablation | difference joint − best single modality, with CIs | single-modality baselines on the same split |

An objective usually names two tasks; the first one named is primary.
If the objective asks for something no tool measures, say so, run the
closest supported analysis, and flag the gap in the report.

# Step 2 — decide the label policy

Labels in `dataset.json → label_columns` are first of all the *yardstick*.

- **Default: no labels in training.** Train self-/cross-modally supervised
  methods (`clip`, `vicreg`, `simclr`, `pca_concat`, `identity`); evaluate
  with labels.
- **Labels allowed in training** (`supcon_clip`) only when the objective
  says labels are available for training, or explicitly asks for the best
  possible classifier. Then (a) keep a label-free model as the comparison,
  (b) mark every label-trained row as such, (c) never present its
  classification score as evidence of what the modalities share.
- **Check how the labels were made** (`DATA.md`). Labels predicted from ONE
  modality (e.g. cell types called from RNA alone) favour that modality's
  representation: a joint model can at best tie on them. Say this when you
  interpret "does adding modality X help?".
- **Text shortcut.** If `profile.json → modalities.<text>.label_predictable_from_words_alone`
  is high (≳ 0.8 balanced accuracy), classifying that label from the text side
  tests word-spotting, not representation quality: judge classification on the
  NON-text side (e.g. the image embedding) and treat retrieval as the
  alignment test.

# Step 3 — fix the baselines before training

Always: each modality alone (`pca_concat` with one input, or `identity` of a
pretrained encoder) and early fusion (`pca_concat` of all inputs). Add the
pretrained zero-shot embedding when a pretrained shared-space encoder exists
for these modalities. Chance levels come with every metric — quote them.

# Step 4 — write the success criterion BEFORE training

Log it as the `objective` decision: concrete, falsifiable, and achievable
with this test set (check class sizes in `profile.json → labels`; a class
with < ~10 test samples cannot carry a conclusion on its own). Examples:

- integration: "the joint embedding's probe balanced accuracy on
  `label_fine` exceeds the best single modality's, with non-overlapping 95%
  CIs; otherwise report that the second modality adds no measurable label
  information";
- retrieval: "image→text recall@5 of the chosen model exceeds the zero-shot
  pretrained model's by more than the width of its 95% CI";
- prediction: "per-sample Pearson r of predicted vs observed target clearly
  above the train-mean baseline (CI excludes it)".

Also state which label column is primary (fine-grained labels are more
informative about what a second modality adds than coarse ones, if their
classes are large enough), and what metric would make you change course.

---
name: preprocessing
description: Choose a preprocess.py spec for each modality (encoder inputs and cross-modal prediction targets) from the profile, not from habit.
---

# When to apply
After the objective decision, before any training. One spec per modality for
the encoders; extra "target" specs only if the objective includes cross-modal
prediction. Log one `preprocessing` decision covering all specs, with the
`profile.json` numbers that justified each.

# Principles
- Everything fitted (feature selection, IDF, PCA/SVD, scaling) is fitted on
  train by the tool. You choose *what*, the tool guarantees *where*.
- Encoder inputs should be compact (tens to a few hundred dimensions) and
  denoised: contrastive encoders on 10⁴–10⁵ raw sparse features overfit and
  are slow.
- Read each `features/<mod>__<spec>.json` after running: dimension,
  explained variance, and for LSI `first_component_corr_with_depth`.

# Count modalities — decide from the profile

Read `profile.json → modalities.<m>`: `fraction_zero`, `library_size`,
`fraction_nonzero_values_equal_1`, `fraction_nonzero_values_le_2`,
`median_overdispersion_top2000`, `features_in_ge_1pct_samples`.

| Evidence | Data type it indicates | Encoder-input spec | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| counts spread over many values, overdispersed, ~10⁴ features (gene expression) | RNA-like | `log1p_hvg2000_pca50` (n_train < ~1,000: `hvg1000_pca30`) | library-size normalisation + log tames depth and skew; HVGs keep the informative genes; PCA denoises |
| ≥ ~0.7 of non-zero values ≤ 2, ≥ ~0.9 zeros, ~10⁵ features (peaks, accessibility) | near-binary, ATAC-like (10x counts each fragment's two cut sites, so "2" usually just means "open") | `tfidf_lsi50_drop1` | TF-IDF weights rare informative peaks; LSI is the standard reduction; the first component tracks sequencing depth |
| `drop1`: check `first_component_corr_with_depth` | | keep `drop1` if \|r\| ≳ 0.7; if \|r\| is small, rerun without it and log that | dropping a biological component would lose signal |
| very few features (< ~200) or already-reduced values | dense | `scale` (optionally `_pcaK`) | nothing to select |

Variants worth trying only if evaluation points to the input: more
components (`pca100`, `lsi100`) when the fine-label probe is far below the
coarse one; `log1p_scale_pca50` when a few very high-variance genes dominate.

## Cross-modal prediction targets (only if the objective asks)
Predict an interpretable, preprocessed version of the target modality — not
raw counts, not the target's own LSI/PCA (those are not "the modality"):
- RNA-like target: `log1p_hvg2000` (continuous; scored by Pearson r).
- ATAC-like target: `binary_top10000` (most-detected peaks, on/off; scored
  by AUROC). Use `binary_top5000` if n_train < ~2,000.

# Image and text modalities

| Situation | Spec | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A pretrained encoder exists whose training data matches the domain (e.g. BiomedCLIP for biomedical figures/captions) and both modalities have it | `biomedclip` for BOTH image and text | in-domain pretraining on far more pairs than we have; the two outputs already share a space, which gives a zero-shot baseline for free |
| Baseline to show what pretraining buys | text `tfidf_svd128`, image `pixels32_pca50` | deliberately simple; any learned model should beat them |
| Images mostly grayscale (`fraction_grayscale`) | no change — the pretrained encoder expects RGB, the tool converts | |

Pretrained features are computed once and cached (`outputs/_cache/`); a
second run with the same spec reads the cache in seconds. The first
encoding of tens of thousands of images can take many minutes on a laptop:
the tool prints progress with elapsed time — use the first lines to estimate
the total, run it in the background if it is long, and wait for the
`features/<mod>__biomedclip.npz` file. It does not count toward the training
budget.

Do NOT clean or mask caption text (e.g. removing modality words) unless the
objective asks for it — but record the text-shortcut number from the profile
(objective skill) because it changes how classification results are read.
---
name: fusion
description: Choose how to combine the modalities (no fusion, early fusion, aligned shared space, supervised alignment, light fine-tuning of a pretrained model), the encoder, and what to compare it against.
---

# When to apply
After preprocessing, before choosing hyperparameters. Log one `fusion`
decision (strategy + baselines) and one `model_selection` decision (method +
encoder) — or a single `fusion` decision if they are inseparable.

# The options (train.py --method)

| Method | What it does | Lecture idea | Gives per-modality embeddings in one space? | Uses labels? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `pca_concat` (1 input) | single-modality baseline: PCA of one modality | PCA | — | no |
| `pca_concat` (all inputs) | early fusion: z-score, weight modalities equally, concatenate, PCA | PCA / early fusion | no (joint only) | no |
| `identity` | use a pretrained encoder's features as they are | foundation model, zero-shot | yes, if the encoder was trained jointly (e.g. BiomedCLIP image + text) | no |
| `clip` | one encoder per modality; paired samples pulled together, other pairs in the batch pushed apart (symmetric InfoNCE) | contrastive / CLIP (L23–L24) | yes | no |
| `vicreg` | one encoder per modality; paired embeddings close + each dimension keeps variance + dimensions decorrelated; no negatives | non-contrastive SSL (L24) | yes | no |
| `supcon_clip` | `clip` + supervised contrastive term: same-label samples are also positives | SupCon (L23) | yes | **yes** |
| `simclr` | ONE modality, two augmented views of each sample | SSL (L24) | — | no |

Encoders (`--encoder`): `mlp` (default for inputs from PCA/LSI/TF-IDF),
`linear` (tiny n, or to test whether nonlinearity matters), `adapter`
(residual MLP starting at the identity: light fine-tuning of pretrained
features; requires input dim = `--dim`, e.g. 512 for BiomedCLIP).

# Decision rules

**1. Always build the baselines** (objective skill): each modality alone and
`pca_concat` of all inputs; `identity` of the pretrained features when they
exist. They cost seconds.

**2. Pick the primary method from the objective and the data:**

| Situation (evidence) | Primary | Why / alternative worth one comparison |
|---|---|---|
| Paired samples, objective includes retrieval or cross-modal prediction, no pretrained shared-space encoder | `clip` with `mlp` encoders | a shared space is required; contrastive alignment is the standard way to get it. Alternative: `vicreg` |
| Same, but small n_train (< ~2,000) or many near-duplicate pairs (duplicate texts, cells of one type that look alike) | `vicreg` | contrastive loss treats look-alike pairs as negatives (false negatives) and is batch-size hungry; VICReg has no negatives. Alternative: `clip` with a smaller batch |
| A pretrained encoder already maps both modalities into one space (`identity` works: retrieval well above chance on val) | `clip` with `--encoder adapter --select-by val_recall` on the pretrained features (= light fine-tuning) | starts exactly at the zero-shot model, and epoch 0 is kept unless an epoch beats it on val matching, so it can only end at or above the zero-shot model on val; cheap. Alternative: `mlp` projection heads on the same features (more capacity, more overfitting risk) |
| Objective is only integration/classification and modalities are unpaired or retrieval is irrelevant | `pca_concat` may already be enough — test `clip`/`vicreg` joint against it | a learned method is justified only if it beats early fusion |
| Objective explicitly allows labels for training | `supcon_clip` next to the label-free primary | report both; the label-free one answers "what do the modalities share?" |
| Only one modality has signal for the objective (e.g. single-modality baseline ≈ joint everywhere) | say so; keep the multimodal model only if it adds retrieval/prediction | |

**3. Embedding size** (`--dim`): ~ the number of meaningful directions —
16–64 for cell types (tens of classes), the pretrained dimension (512) for
an adapter. Bigger is not better for contrastive training at n ~10⁴.

**4. At most one alternative** to the primary in the first round; more only
as a logged iteration that a specific val result motivated.

# Pitfalls to check (and log if relevant)
- **False negatives** in contrastive training: many samples that genuinely
  match each other (same cell type; duplicate captions) are treated as
  negatives. Symptom: retrieval good within class, poor across. VICReg or a
  supervised term changes this — note the label policy.
- **Modality gap**: aligned embeddings can still sit in two separate clouds
  (`collapse.modality_gap_centroid_dist`); retrieval works anyway, but a joint
  embedding computed as their average then mixes two offsets — compare the
  joint vs per-modality probes.
- **Unequal modality strength**: if one modality alone matches the joint
  model, the second adds nothing for that task. That is a result.
---
name: training
description: Size hyperparameters to the data and budget, smoke-test, train, and run the health checks (overfitting, collapse, chance-level matching, temperature) before trusting any embedding.
---

# When to apply
After the fusion decision (log `hyperparameters`), and after every training
run (log `training_check`).

# Defaults and how to adjust them

| Knob | Starting value | Adjust when |
|---|---|---|
| `--batch-size` | 512 for `clip`/`supcon_clip` with n_train ≥ 5,000; 256 below; ≤ n_train/4 | contrastive losses get more negatives from bigger batches; VICReg is fine at 256 |
| `--lr` | 1e-3 (`mlp`, `linear`); 1e-4 (`adapter`: move gently away from a good pretrained start) | loss oscillates → halve; flat from epoch 1 → double once; adapter worse than its start already at epoch 1 → divide by 3–10 |
| `--select-by` | `val_recall` when the objective's primary task is retrieval / cross-modal matching, and always for `adapter`; `val_loss` otherwise | the kept epoch should be the best on what the objective measures; the batch loss can keep falling while matching gets worse |
| `--hidden` / `--layers` | 256 / 2 (`mlp`); 256 / – (`adapter`) | strong overfitting (below) → 128 or `--layers 1`; underfitting on train → 512 |
| `--dropout` | 0.1 | overfitting → 0.2–0.3 |
| `--weight-decay` | 1e-4 | overfitting → 1e-3 |
| `--dim` | fusion skill | |
| `--temperature` | 0.07, learned | stuck → `--fixed-temperature` with 0.1 |
| `--epochs` / `--patience` | 300 / 20 (early stopping on val loss keeps the best epoch) | |
| `--max-minutes` | split the budget: primary ≈ 50%, alternative ≈ 25%, ≥ 25% kept for iterations | |

Precomputed inputs (PCA/LSI/pretrained features) make an epoch take
seconds at n ~ 10⁴, so budget is rarely the binding constraint — overfitting
is. Always run `--smoke` first for each new configuration.

Every learned run also scores **epoch 0**, the model before any update, and
keeps it if no later epoch beats it on `--select-by`. Compare
`summary.val_recall_at_1_initial` with `summary.val_recall_at_1_kept_model`
to see what training actually bought.

# Health checks — read `train_log.json`, `loss.png`, `run_config.json → summary`

| Check | Where | Healthy | Problem → action |
|---|---|---|---|
| Overfitting | train vs val loss curves; `best_epoch` | val loss flattens near train | val loss rises while train falls and `best_epoch` ≲ 10% of epochs run → more dropout/weight decay, smaller `--hidden`, fewer layers, or `vicreg` |
| Matching above chance | `val_recall_at_1` vs `val_recall_at_1_chance`; `summary.val_recall_at_1_kept_model` | many times chance | ≈ chance → inputs not paired correctly, lr wrong, or no shared signal; check the inputs' own baselines before tuning |
| Collapse | `val_embedding_sd_mean`; later `collapse.effective_rank`, `dead_dims` | sd stays well above 0; effective rank ≳ a few | sd → 0 or effective rank ≈ 1 → collapse: for `vicreg` raise the variance weight (not exposed: switch to `clip`), for `clip` check the temperature |
| Temperature | `temperature` column | settles between ~0.01 and ~0.2 | runs to the clamp (0.01) early with rising val loss → `--fixed-temperature` |
| Stop reason | `summary.stop_reason` | early stop or epochs | "time budget" → the model may be undertrained: say so or give it more minutes in an iteration |

|---|---|---|

| Only one modality has signal for the objective (e.g. single-modality baseline ≈ joint everywhere) | say so; keep the multimodal model only if it adds retrieval/prediction | |

as a logged iteration that a specific val result motivated.

  match each other (same cell type; duplicate captions) are treated as
  negatives. Symptom: retrieval good within class, poor across. VICReg or a

  embedding computed as their average then mixes two offsets — compare the
  joint vs per-modality probes.

name: evaluation
description: Choose which evaluate.py tasks measure the objective, compare models on val, report on test, and interpret every metric against its baseline and chance level.
---

# When to apply
After training (on val, to choose), after the choice (on test, to report),
and when writing the results section.

# Pick tasks from the objective

| Objective task (objective skill) | `--tasks` | extra flags |
|---|---|---|
| classification / integration | `structure,collapse` | `--labels` all label columns; read the primary one first |
| clustering | `structure,collapse` | look at ARI/NMI and silhouette, not the probe |
| retrieval | `retrieval,collapse` | (+ `structure` if classification is also asked) |
| cross-modal prediction | `cross` | `--cross a->b:<target spec>,b->a:<target spec>` (targets from preprocessing) |

Run the SAME tasks on every model and baseline, so `compare_runs.py` can
put them side by side. `cross` needs the run to contain an embedding of the
source modality (`z_<src>`): the single-modality baseline of the source gives
the non-multimodal reference ("how well does RNA alone, compressed the same
way, predict ATAC?").

# Val to choose, test to report
1. `evaluate.py --split val` for every model → `compare_runs.py --split val`
   → choose. Log the choice with the val numbers.
2. `evaluate.py --split test` for the chosen model(s) AND the baselines →
   `compare_runs.py --split test --reference <best single-modality baseline>`
   (and once more with `--reference <early fusion or zero-shot>` if that is the
   stronger baseline for a claim) → these numbers go in the report.
If test disagrees with val (e.g. ranking flips within overlapping CIs), say
so — do not switch models because of it.

# Reading each metric

**Classification (`structure`)**
- *Probe balanced accuracy*: a linear classifier on the embedding (fit on
  train). Balanced = mean recall over classes, so a majority class cannot
  hide failures on rare ones. Compare with `chance_balanced_accuracy` and
  the single-modality baselines. Use `probe_per_class_recall` to name the
  classes a representation fails on.
- *kNN balanced accuracy*: does the neighbourhood structure (not just a
  linear direction) carry the label?
- **"Is A better than B?" is answered by the PAIRED difference**
  (`comparison_<split>_vs_<reference>.md`): both models are scored on the same
  samples, so resampling them together removes the shared sample-to-sample
  noise. Overlapping per-model intervals are NOT evidence of no difference —
  never conclude "no proven gain" from them. Report the difference with its CI
  ("+0.05 [+0.02, +0.08]"), and judge size as well as sign: with thousands of
  samples a tiny difference (e.g. +0.004 in per-cell r) can exclude 0 and still
  be practically irrelevant — say so.
- Small classes dominate the noise of balanced accuracy (each class weighs
  the same): name classes with < ~10 evaluated samples as uninterpretable.
- **Name the weakest LARGE class**: from `probe_per_class_recall`, the class
  with the most samples among those with low recall (e.g. < 0.75). A big
  class that is often misclassified matters more to users than a tiny one,
  and it usually points to biologically/visually similar neighbours.
- Labels made from one modality (DATA.md) cap what the other can add —
  read "joint ≈ that modality alone" as expected, not as failure.
- Text shortcut: if the label is predictable from words alone
  (`profile.json`), the text embedding's probe is not evidence of anything —
  and neither is the JOINT probe, because the joint embedding averages in the
  text. Report the non-text side: the `probe_bal_acc[<label>](image)` column
  of `comparison_<split>.md` and the "(image)" rows of the paired table. Do not
  put text-only baselines in a column about classifying from the image.
- `compare_runs.py` shows the joint probe AND each modality's own probe for
  multimodal models (column suffix "(rna)", "(image)", ...). Choose the column
  that answers the objective's question and name it in the report.

**Clustering**: ARI (0 = random, 1 = identical to labels) and NMI; kmeans
uses k = number of classes, so very imbalanced labels depress ARI even for a
good embedding — interpret with the probe. Even when the objective does not
ask for clustering, mention it if the chosen model's ARI is clearly the
worst of the compared models: it means classes are linearly separable but not
grouped into compact clusters, which matters to anyone who will cluster the
embedding.

**Retrieval (`retrieval`)**: recall@k = fraction of queries whose true partner
is in the top k out of `n_candidates`; chance is k / n_candidates. Report
both directions; asymmetry is normal. FOSCTTM = average fraction of
candidates closer than the true partner (0 perfect, 0.5 random) — the most
stable single number for paired cells. Exact-duplicate texts (profile
`duplicate_text_fraction`) put a small ceiling on text-side recall@1.
For paired single cells, recall@1 is naturally low (thousands of cells of the
same type look alike); FOSCTTM and recall@10 are the better summaries.

**Cross-modal prediction (`cross`)**
- Continuous target: *per-sample Pearson r* (does the predicted profile of a
  cell correlate with its observed one?) compared with
  `per_sample_pearson_baseline_train_mean` — the baseline is high because all
  cells share an average profile, so the GAIN over it is the result; *per-
  feature r* (does a gene's predicted level track its observed level across
  cells? baseline 0) and `r2_vs_baseline`.
- Binary target: per-feature AUROC (baseline 0.5) and per-sample AUROC vs the
  train-mean baseline.

**Collapse / geometry (`collapse`)**: effective rank ≪ dim or `dead_dims` > 0
→ partial collapse (training skill). `alignment_paired_sq_dist` should be far
below `alignment_random_pairs_sq_dist`. `modality_gap_centroid_dist` > ~0.5
means two separate clouds (see fusion skill).

**Figures**: `embedding.png` (test) — left: joint embedding coloured by the
primary label; right: both modalities in the shared space with grey lines
joining a few pairs. Describe what is visible (separated classes? mixed
modalities or two clouds?). `comparison_<split>.png` for the report.

# When evaluation should trigger an iteration
- A learned model is below its own baselines on the primary metric → check
  training health first; then try the logged alternative.
- Fine-label probe far below coarse-label probe while coarse is near perfect
  → more input components (preprocessing skill) or larger `--dim`.
- Retrieval far above chance but classification below baselines → the joint
  embedding (average of modalities) may be hurt by a modality gap: compare
  per-modality probes, and consider using the best modality's embedding.
- Adapter never beats zero-shot on val → stop; zero-shot is the answer.
  A very strong zero-shot baseline leaves little headroom: judge a gain
  against the zero-shot CI, and remember it may be inflated by pretraining
  overlap (recommendation skill).
---
name: recommendation
description: Run and report the downstream analyses the objective asked for, then give one consistent recommendation of which representation to use, for what, and with which caveats.
---

# When to apply
After the test evaluation of the chosen model(s) and baselines.

# Downstream analyses
The objective names them (objective skill); each gets its own report
subsection with: the question in plain words, the method in one sentence
(e.g. "a linear classifier trained on the embeddings of training cells"),
the headline number next to its baseline and chance, the 95% CI, and one
sentence of interpretation. At least one downstream analysis is required.

| Downstream task | Evidence to show |
|---|---|
| classification | probe balanced accuracy (+ macro-F1) for chosen model vs every baseline; the 2–3 classes it handles best/worst (`probe_per_class_recall`) |
| clustering | ARI/NMI vs baselines; the embedding figure |
| retrieval | recall@1/5/10 both directions vs chance and vs zero-shot; one sentence on what a miss tends to look like if visible (e.g. same modality, different body part) |
| cross-modal prediction | per-sample r / AUROC vs the train-mean baseline and vs the single-modality baseline embedding; per-feature r and the fraction of features predicted with r > 0.3 |

Log one `downstream` decision summarising the analyses run and their headline
numbers (with file names).

# The recommendation (log `recommendation`)
Answer the objective in one sentence, then:

1. **Which representation, for which use.** It can differ by task — e.g.
   "joint VICReg embedding for cell-type annotation; the RNA encoder alone
   when only RNA is measured" or "fine-tuned adapter for retrieval; the
   zero-shot model is within its CI for modality classification".
2. **The deciding numbers**: the chosen model vs the best baseline on the
   primary metric, as a PAIRED difference with its 95% CI
   (`comparison_test_vs_<baseline>.md`), next to the two values.
3. **Verdict categories** (pick one, use it in the header, Summary and
   Recommendation):
   - *Multimodal helps*: the chosen multimodal representation beats the best
     single-modality / zero-shot baseline on the primary metric, with a paired
     difference whose CI excludes 0 and a size that matters.
   - *Multimodal enables*: no gain on classification, but it provides
     something a single modality cannot (retrieval, cross-modal prediction).
   - *No measurable gain*: the paired difference vs the best baseline has a CI
     that includes 0 (or is too small to matter) — recommend the simpler
     baseline (fewer moving parts), and say what evidence would change this.
   - *Can't tell*: the test set cannot resolve the question (too few samples
     in the relevant classes); say which data would.
4. **Caveats that change how to use it**: label provenance (labels predicted
   from one modality), text shortcuts, label-trained models, duplicates,
   subset size, one donor / one data source, and **pretraining overlap**: if
   a pretrained encoder was trained on data from the same source as this
   dataset (compare `DATA.md` source with what is known about the encoder's
   pretraining data), its zero-shot scores — and anything built on them — may
   be inflated by having seen test samples. State it as a possibility unless
   the overlap can be ruled out; it cannot be measured with these tools.
5. **What would change the recommendation** (one or two concrete items).

Implementation matters: prefer the simplest representation whose paired
difference from the best includes 0 — a frozen pretrained model or PCA is
easier to deploy and audit than a trained encoder.

# Naming numbers consistently
A model with several embeddings (joint, plus one per modality) yields
several "RNA" numbers. In the Summary, Results and Recommendation, "RNA
alone" / "image alone" always means the single-modality BASELINE model. If
you also discuss a multimodal model's own per-modality embedding (e.g. its
RNA encoder), name it explicitly ("the joint model's RNA encoder") and never
put it where a baseline number is expected. The comparison table and the
prose must show the same numbers for the same names.

name: evaluation
description: Choose which evaluate.py tasks measure the objective, compare models on val, report on test, and interpret every metric against its baseline and chance level.
---

# When to apply
After training (on val, to choose), after the choice (on test, to report),
and when writing the results section.

# Pick tasks from the objective

| Objective task (objective skill) | `--tasks` | extra flags |
|---|---|---|
| classification / integration | `structure,collapse` | `--labels` all label columns; read the primary one first |
| clustering | `structure,collapse` | look at ARI/NMI and silhouette, not the probe |
| retrieval | `retrieval,collapse` | (+ `structure` if classification is also asked) |
| cross-modal prediction | `cross` | `--cross a->b:<target spec>,b->a:<target spec>` (targets from preprocessing) |

Run the SAME tasks on every model and baseline, so `compare_runs.py` can
put them side by side. `cross` needs the run to contain an embedding of the
source modality (`z_<src>`): the single-modality baseline of the source gives
the non-multimodal reference ("how well does RNA alone, compressed the same
way, predict ATAC?").

# Val to choose, test to report
1. `evaluate.py --split val` for every model → `compare_runs.py --split val`
   → choose. Log the choice with the val numbers.
2. `evaluate.py --split test` for the chosen model(s) AND the baselines →
   `compare_runs.py --split test --reference <best single-modality baseline>`
   (and once more with `--reference <early fusion or zero-shot>` if that is the
   stronger baseline for a claim) → these numbers go in the report.
If test disagrees with val (e.g. ranking flips within overlapping CIs), say
so — do not switch models because of it.

# Reading each metric

**Classification (`structure`)**
- *Probe balanced accuracy*: a linear classifier on the embedding (fit on
  train). Balanced = mean recall over classes, so a majority class cannot
  hide failures on rare ones. Compare with `chance_balanced_accuracy` and
  the single-modality baselines. Use `probe_per_class_recall` to name the
  classes a representation fails on.
- *kNN balanced accuracy*: does the neighbourhood structure (not just a
  linear direction) carry the label?
- **"Is A better than B?" is answered by the PAIRED difference**
  (`comparison_<split>_vs_<reference>.md`): both models are scored on the same
  samples, so resampling them together removes the shared sample-to-sample
  noise. Overlapping per-model intervals are NOT evidence of no difference —
  never conclude "no proven gain" from them. Report the difference with its CI
  ("+0.05 [+0.02, +0.08]"), and judge size as well as sign: with thousands of
  samples a tiny difference (e.g. +0.004 in per-cell r) can exclude 0 and still
  be practically irrelevant — say so.
- Small classes dominate the noise of balanced accuracy (each class weighs
  the same): name classes with < ~10 evaluated samples as uninterpretable.
- **Name the weakest LARGE class**: from `probe_per_class_recall`, the class
  with the most samples among those with low recall (e.g. < 0.75). A big
  class that is often misclassified matters more to users than a tiny one,
  and it usually points to biologically/visually similar neighbours.
- Labels made from one modality (DATA.md) cap what the other can add —
  read "joint ≈ that modality alone" as expected, not as failure.
- Text shortcut: if the label is predictable from words alone
  (`profile.json`), the text embedding's probe is not evidence of anything —
  and neither is the JOINT probe, because the joint embedding averages in the
  text. Report the non-text side: the `probe_bal_acc[<label>](image)` column
  of `comparison_<split>.md` and the "(image)" rows of the paired table. Do not
  put text-only baselines in a column about classifying from the image.
- `compare_runs.py` shows the joint probe AND each modality's own probe for
  multimodal models (column suffix "(rna)", "(image)", ...). Choose the column
  that answers the objective's question and name it in the report.

**Clustering**: ARI (0 = random, 1 = identical to labels) and NMI; kmeans
uses k = number of classes, so very imbalanced labels depress ARI even for a
good embedding — interpret with the probe. Even when the objective does not
ask for clustering, mention it if the chosen model's ARI is clearly the
worst of the compared models: it means classes are linearly separable but not
grouped into compact clusters, which matters to anyone who will cluster the
embedding.

**Retrieval (`retrieval`)**: recall@k = fraction of queries whose true partner
is in the top k out of `n_candidates`; chance is k / n_candidates. Report
both directions; asymmetry is normal. FOSCTTM = average fraction of
candidates closer than the true partner (0 perfect, 0.5 random) — the most
stable single number for paired cells. Exact-duplicate texts (profile
`duplicate_text_fraction`) put a small ceiling on text-side recall@1.
For paired single cells, recall@1 is naturally low (thousands of cells of the
same type look alike); FOSCTTM and recall@10 are the better summaries.

**Cross-modal prediction (`cross`)**
- Continuous target: *per-sample Pearson r* (does the predicted profile of a
  cell correlate with its observed one?) compared with
  `per_sample_pearson_baseline_train_mean` — the baseline is high because all
  cells share an average profile, so the GAIN over it is the result; *per-
  feature r* (does a gene's predicted level track its observed level across
  cells? baseline 0) and `r2_vs_baseline`.
- Binary target: per-feature AUROC (baseline 0.5) and per-sample AUROC vs the
  train-mean baseline.

**Collapse / geometry (`collapse`)**: effective rank ≪ dim or `dead_dims` > 0
→ partial collapse (training skill). `alignment_paired_sq_dist` should be far
below `alignment_random_pairs_sq_dist`. `modality_gap_centroid_dist` > ~0.5
means two separate clouds (see fusion skill).

**Figures**: `embedding.png` (test) — left: joint embedding coloured by the
primary label; right: both modalities in the shared space with grey lines
joining a few pairs. Describe what is visible (separated classes? mixed
modalities or two clouds?). `comparison_<split>.png` for the report.

# When evaluation should trigger an iteration
- A learned model is below its own baselines on the primary metric → check
  training health first; then try the logged alternative.
- Fine-label probe far below coarse-label probe while coarse is near perfect
  → more input components (preprocessing skill) or larger `--dim`.
- Retrieval far above chance but classification below baselines → the joint
  embedding (average of modalities) may be hurt by a modality gap: compare
  per-modality probes, and consider using the best modality's embedding.
- Adapter never beats zero-shot on val → stop; zero-shot is the answer.
  A very strong zero-shot baseline leaves little headroom: judge a gain
  against the zero-shot CI, and remember it may be inflated by pretraining
  overlap (recommendation skill).

# When to apply
After the test evaluation of the chosen model(s) and baselines.

# Downstream analyses
The objective names them (objective skill); each gets its own report
subsection with: the question in plain words, the method in one sentence
(e.g. "a linear classifier trained on the embeddings of training cells"),
the headline number next to its baseline and chance, the 95% CI, and one
sentence of interpretation. At least one downstream analysis is required.

| Downstream task | Evidence to show |
|---|---|
| classification | probe balanced accuracy (+ macro-F1) for chosen model vs every baseline; the 2–3 classes it handles best/worst (`probe_per_class_recall`) |
| clustering | ARI/NMI vs baselines; the embedding figure |
| retrieval | recall@1/5/10 both directions vs chance and vs zero-shot; one sentence on what a miss tends to look like if visible (e.g. same modality, different body part) |
| cross-modal prediction | per-sample r / AUROC vs the train-mean baseline and vs the single-modality baseline embedding; per-feature r and the fraction of features predicted with r > 0.3 |

Log one `downstream` decision summarising the analyses run and their headline
numbers (with file names).

Answer the objective in one sentence, then:

1. **Which representation, for which use.** It can differ by task — e.g.
   "joint VICReg embedding for cell-type annotation; the RNA encoder alone
   when only RNA is measured" or "fine-tuned adapter for retrieval; the
   zero-shot model is within its CI for modality classification".
2. **The deciding numbers**: the chosen model vs the best baseline on the
   primary metric, as a PAIRED difference with its 95% CI
   (`comparison_test_vs_<baseline>.md`), next to the two values.
3. **Verdict categories** (pick one, use it in the header, Summary and
   Recommendation):
   - *Multimodal helps*: the chosen multimodal representation beats the best
     single-modality / zero-shot baseline on the primary metric, with a paired
     difference whose CI excludes 0 and a size that matters.
   - *Multimodal enables*: no gain on classification, but it provides
     something a single modality cannot (retrieval, cross-modal prediction).
   - *No measurable gain*: the paired difference vs the best baseline has a CI
     that includes 0 (or is too small to matter) — recommend the simpler
     baseline (fewer moving parts), and say what evidence would change this.
   - *Can't tell*: the test set cannot resolve the question (too few samples
     in the relevant classes); say which data would.

   from one modality), text shortcuts, label-trained models, duplicates,
   subset size, one donor / one data source, and **pretraining overlap**: if
   a pretrained encoder was trained on data from the same source as this
   dataset (compare `DATA.md` source with what is known about the encoder's
   pretraining data), its zero-shot scores — and anything built on them — may
   be inflated by having seen test samples. State it as a possibility unless
   the overlap can be ruled out; it cannot be measured with these tools.

difference from the best includes 0 — a frozen pretrained model or PCA is
easier to deploy and audit than a trained encoder.

## 2. Data at a glance

*Profile of both modalities and the label distribution.*

|---|---|---|---|

| Text alone (word counts) | – | – | 0.730 (word-spotting, not image evidence) |
| Early fusion | – | – | 0.694 (joint; includes text) |

- **FOSCTTM:** average fraction of candidates ranked closer than the true partner (0 perfect, 0.5 random).

I've finished the run, and the frozen pretrained BiomedCLIP model is the recommended representation. Nothing I trained did better than it.

On the 2,000 test pairs:

| | Frozen BiomedCLIP | Trained projection model | Pixel-PCA image baseline | Chance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Image→text top-5 retrieval | 0.808 | 0.667 | not defined | 0.0025 |
| Text→image top-5 retrieval | 0.808 | 0.673 | not defined | 0.0025 |
| Modality classification from the image (balanced accuracy) | 0.972 | 0.974 | 0.605 | 0.167 |

- **Retrieval:** the frozen model ranks the true caption first for about half the images. The trained projection model is 14 points worse at top-5, with a paired difference of −0.141 [−0.158, −0.122].
- **Classification:** the trained projection model is indistinguishable from the frozen one (+0.002 [−0.003, +0.008]). I judged classification on the image side only, because words alone predict the label at 0.91.
- **Training outcome:** both fine-tuned adapters (learning rates 1e-4 and 1e-5) never beat the untouched model on validation, so they equal the frozen model. I used about 1.1 minutes of the 20-minute budget.
- **Verdict:** multimodal enables. The shared space gives retrieval, but classification gains nothing over the image alone.
- **Caveat:** BiomedCLIP was pretrained on PubMed Central figure–caption pairs, and this dataset comes from the same source. Its scores may therefore be inflated, and I could not measure that here.
- **PET:** only 13 test images, so its 100% recall (the image-embedding probe) is not interpretable.
